Louis the Fifteenth. A French king who reigned from seventeen fifteen to seventeen seventy-four through a long reign that began with prosperity and military dominance but ended in financial crisis and declining power. Initially beloved by the French people as the Well-Beloved, he gradually squandered his inheritance through costly wars, court extravagance, and inability to reform an ossified absolutist system.

He ascended at age five following the death of his great-grandfather Louis the Fourteenth and was governed through regency until reaching maturity. He initially presided over a period of peace and relative prosperity, earning the epithet the Well-Beloved from his grateful subjects.

Louis the Fifteenth became infatuated with the ambitious courtier Madame de Pompadour, whose influence over royal decisions for over two decades scandalized France and distracted the king from governance. He fought costly wars including the War of Austrian Succession and the Seven Years' War, both of which depleted the royal treasury and yielded little territorial gain for France.

He failed to implement structural reforms to the French tax system, maintaining an archaic system that protected nobility and clergy while crushing the common people. He left the royal finances in catastrophic disorder. The debt crisis and fiscal paralysis he passed to his successor made comprehensive reform impossible and contributed to revolutionary ferment.

His reign witnessed the erosion of French power relative to rival European states, leaving the royal treasury bankrupt—a condition his grandson Louis the Sixteenth inherited and failed to remedy, contributing directly to the French Revolution. He connects to Louis the Fourteenth his great-grandfather and predecessor, whose absolute authority and military glory Louis the Fifteenth failed to match.
